GRADE 2 · CURIOSITY

From marks to a morning.

How can quiet marks on a screen turn into something you can learn?

FOUR LITTLE WONDERS

Where shall we look?

Choose a question. Look for a clue in the picture, then test your first idea against the explanation.

01What could these quiet marks be for?↗02Why does the order of the jobs matter?↗03What happens when each job is followed?↗04How do we know the jobs worked?↗

Start with one question. A question is enough.

LOOK CLOSELY · 01

What could these quiet marks be for?

Look at the screen. Are the marks scattered, or lined up? Find where Little's eyes rest first.

A little explanation & something to try

The marks look like a secret language. They are instructions — tiny written jobs a machine can follow. Alone, one mark does almost nothing. Together in a list, they can build something new.

Try this. Point to one mark, then the next. What changes if you skip one in the middle?

LOOK CLOSELY · 02

Why does the order of the jobs matter?

Find the numbered steps on the notebook. Which job comes first? Which comes last?

A little explanation & something to try

A sequence is a careful order. Job 1 must finish before job 2 begins. If you draw the picture after you place the words, the page looks different than if you reverse those jobs. Order is part of the plan.

Try this. Say three morning jobs out of order. What goes wrong? Put them back in a sequence that works.

LOOK CLOSELY · 03

What happens when each job is followed?

Watch the path from the list to the blank page. Where does a new shape first appear?

A little explanation & something to try

A helper — here, a quiet computer — follows each instruction exactly. One job places a line. The next adds a color wash. The next lays down a word. The page transforms: it changes from blank to pictured.

Try this. Trace the orange path from one job to the page. Which job left the first mark you can see?

LOOK CLOSELY · 04

How do we know the jobs worked?

Compare the blank page on the left with the finished page on the right. What new evidence appears?

A little explanation & something to try

Evidence is a clue you can point to. The blank page had no picture and no sentence. The finished page shows both. That difference is evidence the instructions ran. We infer — we build an idea — that the ordered jobs made the change.

Try this. Name two details that were missing before and are present now. Why are two details stronger than one?

KEEP THE SAME LITTLE WORLD

Let the pictures lead you on.

Follow the marks through the story. Use order as evidence, work out a pretend job list, and explain a discovery in your own words.

A STORY TO EXPLORE

From marks to a morning.

Six close looks. One hidden path from marks to a morning lesson.

One little page at a time.

Quiet marks

Quiet marks

Little Wonderer leans toward a soft screen. The marks are neat, not scribbles. “Are they a secret?” Big Wonderer waits. One mark alone does almost nothing. A list of marks can be instructions — tiny jobs written so a machine can follow them.

Which detail makes the marks look planned instead of accidental?

Jobs in order

Jobs in order

On the notebook, three jobs sit in a line: first, next, then last. That careful order is a sequence. If the last job ran first, the page would look wrong. Little copies the order with a finger. The plan lives in the sequence, not in any single mark.

What can go wrong if two jobs switch places?

Each job runs

Each job runs

A quiet helper follows job one, then job two, then job three. A line lands. A wash of color follows. A word settles into place. The blank page transforms — it changes because each instruction ran in turn. Little watches the path from list to paper.

Which job left the first mark you can point to on the page?

A page appears

A page appears

Left: a blank page. Right: a picture and a short sentence. That difference is evidence the jobs worked. Little builds an inference: the ordered instructions made the finished page. One detail could be luck. Two matching changes are harder to ignore.

Which two details are the strongest evidence that a change happened?

Marks mean a lesson

Marks mean a lesson

Little returns to the first screen of marks. Beside it rests a finished morning sheet — a lesson ready to use. The earlier guess (“secret scribbles”) no longer fits. The marks were a plan to transform instructions into something you can learn.

How did comparing the first marks with the finished sheet change Little's idea?

Keep one question

Keep one question

The lesson is here: words, a picture, a puzzle to try. Code became a daily morning. Little keeps one precise question: What else could a careful sequence of jobs become? Another picture? A song of clicks? The next list is waiting.

What new evidence could support or challenge the idea that order matters?

COMPARE TWO INTERVALS

Job counts grow across three pretend mornings: 12, then 19, then 31. Find the change from morning 1 to 2 and from morning 2 to 3. Which change is greater, and by how much?

19 − 12 = ___; 31 − 19 = ___; ___ − ___ =  

A small hint

Find both changes first. Then subtract the smaller change from the greater one.

JOIN THE JOBS

One sequence uses 14 picture jobs and 9 word jobs. After that, 6 check jobs still wait. How many jobs are done before the checks? How many jobs in all?

14 + 9 = ___; ___ + 6 =  

A small hint

Add the picture and word jobs first. Then add the checks.

TEST A CLAIM

Someone says the total change from morning 1 to morning 3 is 18. Use the table to decide whether the claim is true and correct it.

31 − 12 =  

A small hint

Subtract the first value from the last value. Compare your result with 18.

For grown-ups & print downloads

These are imagined, enlarged scenes about how ordered instructions (code) can become a printed lesson — not a coding tutorial, IDE walkthrough, or claim about any one programming language. 'Instructions,' 'sequence,' and 'transform' are kid-sized models. The helper/computer is schematic. Job counts and morning totals are invented for math and independent of art scale. Screens and notebooks in the plates are props, not real interfaces to copy. Support pronunciation, invented spelling or dictation as useful. Keep adult guidance in this key or collapsed details.

About 15 min: look, read six short beats, then talk. No independent reading required.
